summary: The first-person travel party sails from Miletus through Tyre and Caesarea toward Jerusalem. Disciples warn Paul through the Spirit, Philip's four prophetic daughters host the group, and Agabus binds himself with Paul's belt to dramatize coming arrest. Paul interprets the warnings as preparation, not prohibition, and accepts possible death. In Jerusalem James and the elders celebrate Gentile mission while describing thousands of Jewish believers zealous for Torah. To answer rumors that Paul teaches Jews to abandon Moses, he joins four men in purification. Diaspora opponents falsely accuse him of bringing Trophimus into the temple; a crowd attacks, Roman soldiers intervene, and Paul identifies himself in Greek before requesting permission to address the people in the local Semitic language.
whyItMatters: The chapter resists the story that Gentile mission required Jewish believers to stop being Jewish. Paul participates in purification, the Jerusalem believers remain Torah-zealous, and the actual temple charge is based on an assumption. Spirit-led obedience is also complex: prophecy accurately names danger, while faithful hearers differ over whether danger means ‘do not go’ or ‘go prepared.’

context.author: The anonymous narrator of Luke–Acts, traditionally Luke, now using first-person plural for the voyage and arrival
context.audience: Readers navigating prophecy, Torah-observant Jewish belief, temple boundaries, rumor, crowd violence, and Roman custody
context.date: Acts is commonly dated around AD 80–90, with dates in the 60s and later also argued; the chapter narrates Paul's final Jerusalem visit
context.setting: Coastal voyage, Tyre, Caesarea, Jerusalem community, and the temple complex
context.literaryForm: First-person travel narrative, prophetic warning, leadership consultation, purification narrative, riot, and arrest

outline.heading: Disciples and prophets warn Paul along the voyage
outline.note: Disciples at Tyre tell Paul not to go up; Agabus binds his own hands and feet with Paul's belt; Paul is ready to die

outline.heading: Jerusalem leaders receive Paul and propose public purification
outline.note: James and the elders glorify God and tell Paul to purify himself with four men under a vow; he does so in the temple

outline.heading: A false temple accusation provokes mob violence and Roman arrest
outline.note: Jews from Asia seize Paul in the temple, claiming he brought Greeks in; the crowd beats him until the commanding officer arrests him

outline.heading: Paul identifies himself and asks to address the crowd
outline.note: The officer asks 'Do you know Greek' and takes Paul for the Egyptian; Paul says he is a Jew from Tarsus

keyVerses.text: Then Paul answered, “What are you doing, weeping and breaking my heart? For I am ready not only to be bound, but also to die at Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus.”
keyVerses.why: Paul interprets prophetic danger through costly readiness rather than absence of emotion.

keyVerses.text: They, when they heard it, glorified God. They said to him, “You see, brother, how many thousands there are among the Jews of those who have believed, and they are all zealous for the law.
keyVerses.why: Acts explicitly depicts a large Jesus-believing Jewish community continuing Torah zeal.

keyVerses.text: But Paul said, “I am a Jew from Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of no insignificant city. I beg you, allow me to speak to the people.”
keyVerses.why: Paul names Jewish and civic identity in fluent Greek before shifting languages for his defense.

questions.question: Do the Spirit's warnings mean Paul disobeys by going to Jerusalem?
questions.answer: At Tyre disciples ‘through the Spirit’ tell Paul not to go; at Caesarea Agabus predicts binding, and companions plead with Paul. Yet earlier the Spirit testified that bonds awaited (20:23), and Paul understands himself as compelled toward Jerusalem (‘bound by the Spirit,’ 20:22). Some readers see disobedience; others distinguish a divine prediction from the disciples' protective inference. Acts never explicitly condemns Paul's choice and later gives him divine encouragement.

questions.question: Why mention Philip's four unmarried daughters who prophesy?
questions.answer: Many readers see them as fulfilling Pentecost's promise that ‘your daughters will prophesy’ (2:17); they show charismatic ministry located in a household beyond Jerusalem. Parthenoi can mean virgins or unmarried daughters. Luke does not preserve their words, which is a frustrating narrative silence, but he plainly identifies their ongoing prophetic activity before introducing Agabus's enacted prophecy.

questions.question: What is Agabus doing with Paul's belt?
questions.answer: Like prophets in Israel's Scriptures (Jeremiah 27:2), Agabus performs a sign-act: he binds his own hands and feet and says the Holy Spirit predicts that the belt's owner will be bound and handed to Gentiles. The later arrest broadly fulfills the image, though a Jewish crowd seizes Paul and Romans bind him. Prophetic speech can be truthful without functioning as a stenographic preview of every agent and step.

questions.question: What does ‘The Lord’s will be done’ mean here?
questions.answer: After failing to persuade Paul, the companions become quiet and entrust the outcome to God's will. The phrase does not prove which prior interpretation of the prophecies was correct, nor does it make grief faithless. It is a relinquishment of control in a situation where everyone seeks faithfulness but discerns the warning differently.

questions.question: Does Acts say Jewish believers should abandon Torah?
questions.answer: No. James and the elders describe ‘myriads’—literally tens of thousands or simply a very great number—of believing Jews who are zealous for Torah. The rumor says Paul teaches diaspora Jews to apostatize from Moses; the leaders' plan is meant to demonstrate that he himself walks orderly and keeps Torah. The Jerusalem decision concerns Gentiles, whose distinct instructions are repeated.

questions.question: What purification does Paul sponsor?
questions.answer: Four men have a vow, probably Nazirite-related (compare Numbers 6:18), and Paul joins their purification and pays expenses so they can shave their heads and complete offerings. The compressed details are debated, but the public act occurs under James's advice and demonstrates solidarity with Jewish practice. Since Paul calls himself a Jew (21:39), most readers do not recast it as Paul pretending to be Jewish for optics.

questions.question: Did Paul bring Trophimus into the forbidden temple area?
questions.answer: No evidence is produced. Diaspora Jews had previously seen Paul with Trophimus the Ephesian in the city and ‘supposed’ Paul brought him inside. Temple warning inscriptions threatened death to Gentiles crossing the inner boundary (Josephus, Antiquities 15.11.5), so the accusation was explosive. Luke carefully distinguishes observation from inference.

questions.question: Who is the ‘Egyptian’ the commander mistakes Paul for?
questions.answer: Josephus also describes (Jewish War 2.13.5) an Egyptian prophetic leader who gathered followers at the Mount of Olives and was defeated by the governor Felix, though his numbers differ from Acts' four thousand sicarii. The commander assumes Paul is that fugitive until Paul's Greek and Tarsian civic identity surprise him.

questions.question: What language does Paul use to address the crowd?
questions.answer: The text says Hebraidi dialektō, ‘in the Hebrew dialect/language.’ In this first-century Jerusalem setting it is often understood as Aramaic, though a form of Hebrew remains possible and the scholarly question should not be hidden. Luke highlights Paul's code-switching: Greek to the Roman commander, then the audience's Semitic speech to fellow Jews.

glossary.def: Greek ‘tens of thousands,’ sometimes used for an immense number rather than an audited count.
Ritual preparation associated here with vows and temple participation.
‘In the Hebrew dialect/language,’ commonly understood here as Aramaic but debated.
